sections.h2: What kind of city is Revere, Massachusetts?
sections.html:
Revere is a dense coastal city in Suffolk County, about five miles northeast of downtown Boston, and it is the end of the MBTA Blue Line. The 2020 census counted 62,186 people on 10.13 square miles, of which 4.43 square miles are water, so most of the city is marsh, beach and harbor edge.

Neighbors are Winthrop, Chelsea, East Boston, Everett, Malden, Saugus and Lynn, with Massachusetts Bay to the east. After the 2020 census Revere was reported as the fastest-growing city in the state, though the later population estimate on Wikipedia, 60,702 for 2024, is lower than the census count.

For a seller, the useful point is how packed the city is: roughly 10,900 people per square mile, so lots are tight, and several districts mix single-family and multi-family houses.

sections.h2: Which Revere neighborhoods do buyers ask about?
sections.html:
Revere is organized around a handful of districts, each with a different housing mix:

  • Beachmont: the eastern edge near East Boston's Orient Heights, with single and multi-family homes and a Blue Line stop.
  • Revere Beach Boulevard: apartment complexes, restaurants and some single-family houses along the three-mile beach, with newer development adding luxury apartments.
  • Point of Pines and Oak Island: the north end of the beach, mostly single and multi-family homes beside the marsh and wetlands.
  • Shirley Avenue: the most ethnically diverse part of the city, with ethnic groceries, restaurants and community services.
  • Broadway and Revere Street: the central civic and commercial arteries that connect City Hall to the beach.
  • West Revere: single and multi-family homes plus the Squire Road business district with large shopping plazas and hotels.

Matching the right buyer to the right district helps a listing: a beachfront condo and a West Revere two-family attract different people.

sections.h2: How did Revere's history shape what is for sale today?
sections.html:
Revere began as Rumney Marsh, was part of Boston from 1632 and then Chelsea, and split off as North Chelsea in 1846. In 1871 it took the name Revere after Paul Revere. Its beach became a public destination in 1896 when the Metropolitan Park Commission took over management.

Railroad lines, first the Eastern Railroad in 1838 and then the Boston, Revere Beach and Lynn Railroad in 1875, set off rapid growth, and the population rose from 5,668 in 1890 to 18,219 in 1910 and 28,823 in 1920.

That first boom is when most of Revere filled in. A later wave of growth pushed the city from 47,283 people in 2000 to 62,186 in 2020.

sections.h2: What does the Blue Line and the road system mean for Revere sellers?
sections.html:
The Blue Line ends in Revere, with three stations: Wonderland, Revere Beach and Beachmont. Houses within walking distance of a station can be easier to market to commuters who work in Boston.

U.S. Route 1 and state routes 1A, 16, 60, 107 and 145 run through the city.

When you list or sell, mention the station name and the walking time. Buyers searching for a Blue Line home compare those details first.

sections.h2: Who works in Revere and what is changing?
sections.html:
According to Revere's 2021 budget as quoted on Wikipedia, the leading employers are supermarkets and health or care operations: Market Basket (210 employees), Mass General Hospital (200), Price Rite (183), Lighthouse Nursing (182), Target (170) and Stop & Shop on Squire Road (150).

The city's 2018 master plan, "Next Stop, Revere," set goals for workforce, small business and science and technology industries over 10 to 20 years.

The biggest recent site change is Wonderland Greyhound Park. Greyhound racing ended there in 2009, the city took the land by eminent domain in 2022, and ground was broken on a new Revere High School at the site in August 2025.

sections.h2: What should Revere sellers know about weather and water?
sections.html:
Revere sits only about 20 feet above sea level and has marsh and ocean on several sides. Two events from its record show why buyers pay attention to storms: the Blizzard of 1978 destroyed many of the beach's remaining businesses, and an EF2 tornado came through Chelsea and into Revere on July 28, 2014, damaging many buildings including City Hall. It was the first tornado to hit Suffolk County since National Weather Service records began in 1950.

Wikipedia describes the year-round range as roughly 23 to 82 degrees Fahrenheit, with snow lasting about five months and the muggiest stretch running from mid-June to late September.

We did not find a city page on flood zones that we could open, so we make no flood claims here. If your house is near the beach or the marsh, ask your insurer and the city building office about flood zone status before listing, so you know the answer before a buyer asks.

sections.h2: What do you have to do before closing a Revere house sale?
sections.html:
Revere sellers follow state sale rules. The Department of Fire Services says you must obtain a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing the smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the requirements for a sale or transfer. Alarms that are more than ten years old, or have no date, must be replaced. The fire department charges for the inspection, so call as soon as a closing date is set. See the Mass.gov guidance.

Massachusetts also taxes deeds by statute. The base rate in G.L. c. 64D, section 1 is $2 per $500 of price.

On the tax side, Revere's Assessors Department is at 281 Broadway and answers at 781-286-8170, and the city lists senior, veteran, blind and hardship exemptions on its assessors page. Each requires ownership and occupancy, and if the property is in a trust the applicant must be both trustee and beneficiary or hold a life estate.

sections.h2: What can you do if your Revere assessment looks too high?
sections.html:
• Pay every tax installment on time. The Appellate Tax Board treats timely payment as a condition for hearing an appeal.
  • File an abatement application with the assessors by the first installment due date printed on your bill.
  • Wait up to three months for a decision, then appeal to the board within three months of that decision or of the deemed denial.
  • Bring comparable sales and photographs of similar nearby houses.

Because the burden is on the owner, a short, evidence-based case does better than a general complaint. The board's guide explains each step.

sections.h2: What are your options if you want to sell a Revere house?
sections.html:
A traditional listing, a sale on your own and a cash sale are the three routes. Which fits depends on repairs, timing and how much effort you can give.

  • A listing exposes the house to the most buyers but brings showings, inspection negotiations and a timeline set by the buyer's lender.
  • A cash sale can close on a schedule you choose, and the buyer takes the house in its present condition.

If your house needs work, a cash buyer may make more sense than spending months on repairs, and you can compare both routes before deciding.

faqs.a: Revere is in Suffolk County, about five miles northeast of downtown Boston.

faqs.q: How many people live in Revere?
faqs.a: The 2020 census counted 62,186 residents. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate shown at the top of this page is 60,141.
The Blue Line ends in Revere with stations at Wonderland, Revere Beach and Beachmont.

faqs.q: Do I need a smoke and CO certificate to sell in Revere?
faqs.a: Yes. Massachusetts requires a certificate of compliance from the local fire department for a sale or transfer of a home.

faqs.q: Who handles property assessments in Revere?
faqs.a: The Assessors Department at 281 Broadway, reachable at 781-286-8170 or assessors@revere.org.

faqs.q: Did a tornado ever hit Revere?
faqs.a: Yes. An EF2 tornado struck Revere on July 28, 2014, damaging many buildings including City Hall.
